summary: Describes a URN namespace for Object Identifiers, letting those dotted numbers be written as URNs. It is informational and replaces RFC 3001.

plainLanguage.summary: Some things have long dotted-number names. This gives them a standard way to be written like web-style names.

questions: how to write an oid as a urn
what is the oid urn namespace
what characters are allowed in an oid urn
subtitle: How to write an Object Identifier, such as 1.3.6.1, as a URN of the form urn:oid:1.3.6.1.

tldr.problem: Object Identifiers (OIDs) are dotted numbers that name things in a global tree, but they had no standard way to appear as Uniform Resource Names.
tldr.mechanism: The memo registers a formal URN namespace called "oid". The part after the prefix is the OID's digits separated by periods, with no leading zeros.
tldr.outcome: OIDs can be written as names like urn:oid:1.3.6.1. No resolution mechanism is defined. The memo is Informational and obsoletes RFC 3001.

today: RFC 3061 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 3001. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Object Identifiers as URNs
sections.content:
An Object Identifier (OID) is a tree of nodes, where each node is a sequence of digits. Once an entity is given a node, it has sole discretion to hand out sub-trees below that node.

The memo gives examples such as 1.3.6.1 (the Internet OID) and 1.3.6.1.4.1 (IANA-assigned company OIDs, used for private MIBs). This document specifies the oid URN namespace, which encodes an OID as defined in ASN.1 as a URI. It is a formal namespace and it obsoletes RFC 3001.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a huge family tree where every branch has a number. This memo says how to write a branch's number so it can be used like a web-style name.

sections.title: The Identifier Syntax
sections.content:
The namespace-specific part of the name follows the string encoding in RFC 1778 section 2.15: digits separated by periods, most significant digit on the left. It is limited to the digits 0-9 and the . character, with no leading zeros. The name must never contain the human-readable description of a node.

The ABNF is short: an oid is a number followed by any number of . and another number. A number is a single digit, or a first digit from 1 to 9 followed by more digits.

Lexical equivalence is an exact string match. The memo expects no changes to the syntax, since OIDs have been standardized with no changes for many years.
sections.plainLanguage: A name is just numbers with dots between them. No spare zeros at the front, no words, and two names are the same only if they look exactly the same.

sections.title: Assignment, Uniqueness and Resolution
sections.content:
The registrant is ISO/IEC JTC 1 SubCommittee 6, which interprets the ASN.1 specification that is the real authority. Once an OID is assigned to an entity, that entity can create and assign new OIDs below it. The top three levels are pre-assigned: 0 for ITU-T, 1 for ISO, and 2 for joint ISO/ITU-T assignment.

The URN namespace inherits the OID rules: each OID is unique and is never reassigned or reused. No resolution mechanism is defined at this time, and there is no validation mechanism. The scope is global.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever owns a branch can hand out smaller branches below it, and a number is never given out twice. Nobody built a lookup service for these names yet.

sections.title: Examples and Security
sections.content:
The examples are urn:oid:1.3.6.1, urn:oid:1.3.6.1.4.1, urn:oid:1.3.6.1.2.1.27 and URN:OID:0.9.2342.19200300.100.4. The last shows that the prefix may be written in capitals.

The security section says there is nothing beyond what is already inherent in using unverifiable OIDs.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing the name is just putting urn:oid: in front of the numbers. Nothing here checks that a number really belongs to anyone.

references.text: Mealling, M., "A URN Namespace of Object Identifiers", RFC 3001, November 2000.
Howes, T., Kille, S., Yeong, W. and C. Robbins, "The String Representation of Standard Attribute Syntaxes", RFC 1778, March 1995.
